name: Glow Protocol
lead: Glow Protocol, also sold as the GLOW blend, is a vendor-assembled peptide blend marketed online for skin quality. The usual listing combines GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 in one vial, with GHK-Cu making up most of the contents.[1][2] People take an interest in it hoping for a firmer, brighter, lit-from-within complexion and faster recovery after skin or tissue stress, drawing on GHK-Cu's association with collagen and wound-repair research.[1][3]

GHK-Cu is a copper-binding tripeptide isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart in the 1970s; laboratory work reported that it boosted collagen production in skin fibroblasts, and it appears in cosmetic anti-aging and hair products as copper tripeptide-1.[3] BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid peptide described in 1993 by Predrag Sikiric and studied mainly in animals for tendon, gut and wound healing.[4] TB-500 is a synthetic peptide based on an active region of thymosin beta-4, a protein that has been tested in phase 2 wound-healing trials.[5]

Vendors label the blend research use only.[1][2] Research on the individual peptides is mostly in cells and animals, and no published human study has tested the three-peptide combination.[1] Online interest has grown through video platforms and wellness forums, where before-and-after images are a common form of promotion.[1]

chain: GHK-Cu studied for collagen and wound repair; BPC-157 and TB-500 for tissue healing
Users expect better skin recovery and firmness
angle.text: People are drawn to the blend for a firmer, brighter complexion. The reasoning rests on GHK-Cu's collagen research and on repair studies of the other two peptides.

infobox: Sold as research use only; not approved as a drug or cosmetic[1]

paras: Most listings describe a vial dominated by GHK-Cu with smaller amounts of BPC-157 and TB-500, around 70 mg in total.[1][2] Some sellers list variants that add other peptides such as KPV, and contents differ between sellers.[2]

GHK-Cu: plasma levels reportedly fall with age, from about 200 ng/ml at 20 to about 80 ng/ml at 60. Lab work from the late 1980s found collagen and glycosaminoglycan increases, and rabbit, rat, mouse and pig wound studies reported better wound contraction; several small, short facial studies suggested firming and anti-wrinkle effects, though the literature calls for further research.[3]

BPC-157: Animal studies suggest protective and healing effects including on tendons and ligaments, while human evidence is described as very limited, with a retrospective study of 12 patients with knee pain, a pilot study on interstitial cystitis and an unreported phase I trial.[4]

TB-500: a synthetic version of an active region of thymosin beta-4. The full protein sped healing of pressure ulcers, venous ulcers and epidermolysis bullosa in phase 2 trials and was reported safe and well tolerated there.[5]

The blend is not approved by the FDA as a drug or cosmetic.[1] An FDA advisory committee reviewed BPC-157 and TB-500 in July 2026 on whether licensed pharmacies may compound them, and FDA staff noted limited quality, safety and effectiveness data for BPC-157.[1] The World Anti-Doping Agency bans BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4.[4][5] Wikipedia also reports concern among researchers that BPC-157's promotion of new blood vessel growth could in theory affect tumour growth, and that health authorities discourage use because human safety data is insufficient.[4]

No studies found of the three-peptide blend. Research on GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 individually is mostly in cells and animals and concerns healing after injury; small facial studies of GHK-Cu and phase 2 wound trials of thymosin beta-4 are described above.[1][3][5]

timeline.event: Loren Pickart isolates GHK-Cu from human plasma albumin.[3]
FDA advisory committee reviews BPC-157 and TB-500 on pharmacy compounding.[1]

card.summary: A vendor blend of GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 that people use hoping for firmer, brighter-looking skin.
card.note: Sold as research use only; not FDA-approved; contents vary by vendor.

quick.overview:
Glow Protocol is an online peptide blend, usually GHK-Cu plus BPC-157 and TB-500, marketed for skin glow and recovery.

Users look to it for firmer, brighter skin, citing GHK-Cu's collagen research.
quick.mechanism: GHK-Cu is studied for collagen and wound repair; BPC-157 and TB-500 for tissue repair in animals. The combination itself has not been studied in people.
quick.risks: Sold as research use only and not approved as a drug or cosmetic. Contents and purity vary by vendor, and FDA staff have noted limited safety data for BPC-157.
